title: Kindness Missions
goal: Your kid learns to spot small chances to be kind, like a seat someone needs or a neighbour carrying too much, and to act on them without being asked. They take on real missions, notice how each one lands, and keep the ones that become habits, the kind you see when nobody's watching.
need: Everyday places: the bus, the store, the street, home
A notebook for the mission log
A week or two, a few missions at a time

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is turning kindness into a chore you assign. Your job is to point out the chances, let them choose, and say exactly what you saw when they act on their own.

plan.what: Spot the chances and choose missions (Steps 1 and 2).
Do the missions and notice how they land (Steps 3 and 4).
Keep the ones that became habits (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They only want to do it for praise or a reward
troubleshoot.a: Try a secret mission, where nobody knows who did it. The feeling afterwards is the real reward.
That's fine, and it still counts. Offering kindly and accepting a no are both part of the mission.
Start at home and with people they know, then try one stranger mission together, side by side.

lesson.text: Most kindness isn't planned. It's noticing someone who needs something, right now, and acting before the moment passes. The missions are practice for that moment.
lesson.before: 'Someone else will give him their seat.'

model.line: An older man standing on the city bus.
He stood up and gave him his seat.
The man thanked him, and said he doesn't see that much anymore.
As he got off, the man gave him $5 for his kindness.

lesson.modelNote: He didn't give up his seat for a reward. He didn't know one was coming. The $5 was a surprise. What he kept was knowing his small choice made someone's day.

steps.title: Spot the chances
steps.why: Kindness starts with noticing. Most chances last a few seconds, and kids who look for them see many more.
steps.kid: On a walk, a bus ride or a trip to the store, your kid looks for people who could use a hand, using the Where to look card in the Kindness Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Point out quietly what you see: 'That lady has a lot of bags.' 'Nobody's sitting with him.' Then let them decide what to do.
ask: Who could use a hand right now?
What would make their day a little easier?
steps.tip: Buses, doors and checkout lines are full of small chances. They pass quickly, so noticing is the skill.

levels.explore: Spot one person on a walk who could use help, and tell a parent.
levels.develop: Spot three chances in one outing, and write them down.
levels.extend: Spot a chance that most people walk past, and say why it's easy to miss.

steps.title: Choose your missions
steps.why: A mission they choose feels like theirs. One you assign feels like a chore.
steps.kid: Your kid picks three missions to try this week from the Mission ideas card, including one for someone at home, one for someone they know and one for a stranger.
steps.you: Help them pick missions that fit their age and comfort. A stranger mission happens with you nearby, in public: never into someone's car or home.
ask: Which mission sounds fun to try?
Who would you most like to surprise?
steps.tip: Mix easy and hard. One small win makes the harder mission feel possible.

levels.explore: Pick one mission for someone at home.
levels.develop: Pick three missions: home, someone you know, and a stranger.
levels.extend: Invent a mission of your own for someone who's often overlooked.

steps.title: Do the mission
steps.why: Kindness only counts when it happens. Doing it, even awkwardly, is the whole point.
steps.kid: Your kid does each mission, using the How to do it card: notice, offer, and accept the answer, even if it's no thanks.
steps.you: Stay close for stranger missions, and let them speak for themselves. Don't jump in to help them say it.
ask: What will you do if they say no thanks?
steps.tip: Offer, don't push. 'Would you like my seat?' leaves room for the other person to say no.

levels.explore: Do one mission with a parent right beside you.
levels.develop: Do all three of your missions this week.
levels.extend: Do a secret mission, where nobody knows it was you.

steps.title: Notice how it landed
steps.why: Seeing what a small act did for someone is what turns a mission into a habit.
steps.kid: After each mission, your kid writes in My kindness log at the end of the guide what they did, how the person reacted, and how they felt.
steps.you: Ask about the other person first, then about them: 'How did he look?' before 'How did you feel?'
steps.tip: Sometimes the reaction is big, sometimes it's nothing. Both count. The kindness was in the doing.

levels.explore: Tell a parent what happened, and draw the person's face.
levels.develop: Log each mission: what you did, their reaction and your feeling.
levels.extend: Log it, and notice whether kindness spread, like someone else helping too.

steps.title: Keep the keepers
steps.why: The goal isn't a list of good deeds. It's a kid who does them without a list.
steps.kid: At the end, your kid looks back through the log and picks two missions to keep doing on their own, using the Keep it card.
steps.you: Name it when you see a keeper happen without a reminder. That's the moment the habit is real.
ask: Which one will you keep doing?
steps.tip: A kind habit sticks best when it's attached to something they already do, like every bus ride, or every time you leave a store.

levels.explore: Pick one kind thing to keep doing every day.
levels.develop: Pick two keepers, and when you'll do them.
levels.extend: Pick your keepers, then show someone at home how to do one with you.

reference.intro: Where to look, what to try, and how to make it stick.

a kind act nobody knows was you

conclusion.headline: They act on kindness without being asked.
conclusion.text: Keep an eye on the next bus ride or store trip. If they're the one who spots the full hands or the empty seat, and does something about it, the missions have become a habit.
conclusion.celebrate: When you see them do it on their own, say: 'You gave him your seat before anyone asked. That was kind, and it was your idea.'
extensions: Plan a family kindness day for a neighbour
Find out what a local shelter or food bank needs, and help
Write thank-you notes to people who help your family often
Notice a kindness someone does for you this week, and pass the same one on to someone else

signs: They offer help to strangers on their own
They notice who's been left out
They do a job at home before anyone asks
makeItReal: On your next bus ride, walk or trip to the store, look for one chance to be kind together. Let them choose what to do, and let them be the one who does it.

fromHome.text: Coming home on the city bus, my son gave his seat to an older man. The man was impressed. He thanked him, and told him he doesn't see many young people being so kind these days. When my son was about to get off, the man gave him $5 for his kindness.
